To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the knots formed inside a viral capsid are not formed during the extraction from the capsid, but rather while the DNA is inside the viral capsids.

(1) the knotting probability and knot complexity of DNA inside the capsid of a tailless mutant phage is much higher than that of DNA extracted from the capsid; (2) Monte Carlo simulations of the knotting of equilaterally polygonal chains in confined volumes reproduce the experimental knotting probability and the knot complexity; (3) the knotting of DNA inside the viral capsids is mainly driven by the effects of the confinement.

(i) the knotting of double-stranded DNA confined to restricted volumes is highly probable and (ii) the knotting probability and the crossing number of the knots formed are strongly affected by the volume in which the chain is confined.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of knots in DNA molecules confined in small volumes.
the formation of DNA knots in the confined environment of the phage capsid.
the knotting probability of DNA confined in restricted volumes, and we conclude that knotting probability of a closed chain confined to a tightly restricted volume is high.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the knots formed in the P4 tail-less mutant are a consequence of the confined volume of the capsid.

, in the case of DNA molecules inside the viral capsids, the probability of forming a knot is higher and the knotting process results in knots with a higher crossing numbers than in the case of free molecules in solution.
the P4 tail-less mutant is a unique case of DNA packing inside a viral capsid, and that the DNA knots are a consequence of a unique combination of DNA length, capsid size, and DNA flexibility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the knotting of DNA in confined volumes is a stochastic process, where the knotting probability depends on the confinement volume and the number of crossings of the knots depends on the confinement geometry.
knotting of DNA molecules in confined volumes is a stochastic process that depends on the size of the confining volume and the size of the molecule.
the knotting probability of a DNA molecule inside a confined volume is much higher than the knotting probability outside of it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
knotting probability and the complexity of the resulting knots can be increased by restricting the volume available for the DNA to move inside.
the formation of knotted DNA inside the phage capsid is not a consequence of a random entangling process, but rather the result of a specific process of knotting that occurs in a restricted volume.
confinement is the key factor in DNA knotting in the capsid.
